content: Juliet Hounsome, Andrew Jones, Michelle Maden, Alejandro Calvillo, Suparna Ghosh-Jerath, Maria João Gregório, Fiona Sing, and Boyd Swinburn declared no conflicts of interest. Their declarations were deemed not applicable to the guideline development process. Lauren McGale disclosed her employment as a research assistant on the SWITCH study at the University of Liverpool, which was funded by the American Beverage Association (ABA). She clarified that the funding was awarded to the university, and she was neither involved in the funding application nor named as an investigator. During her role, she was responsible for participant recruitment and data collection (including running probe days). She did not receive any honorarium from the ABA, and her involvement in the SWITCH trial was not considered a conflict of interest for the guideline development process. Huda Mustafa Al Hourani declared no conflicts of interest, which were deemed not applicable. Gershim Asiki disclosed receiving a research grant from the International Development Research Centre (IDRC) in Canada in 2019 to conduct research on food environments, policy benchmarking in Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda, and mapping food promotion to children in schools, retail outlets, and on TV/radio in Kenya. This declaration was not considered a conflict of interest for his role as an external peer reviewer, given the funding source and research topics. Key characteristics of policies evaluated in studies included in a systematic review on the effectiveness of food marketing restrictions for children were outlined. Examples include: 1. Australian Children’s Television Standards (1984): A mandatory policy targeting children aged 6–13 years, regulating the use of promotions, popular characters, and premium offers in advertisements during designated children’s programming. 2. Australian Food and Grocery Council’s Quick Service Restaurant Initiative (2009): A voluntary policy targeting children under 14 years, with defined nutrition criteria for children’s meals and restrictions on marketing in media primarily directed at children. 3. Canadian Children’s Food and Beverage Advertising Initiative (2007): A voluntary policy targeting children under 12 years, with company-specific nutrition standards and restrictions on advertising in media where children make up 35% or more of the audience. 4. Chile’s Food Labeling and Advertising Regulation (2016, updated 2018): A mandatory policy targeting children under 14 years, prohibiting the use of celebrities, cartoons, toys, and other child-directed marketing techniques for products high in sugar, fat, or salt. 5. EU Pledge (2007, updated 2014): A voluntary policy targeting children under 12 years, restricting advertising of products that do not meet specific nutrition criteria in media where children make up more than 35% of the audience. 6. Mexican Self-Regulation Code (2009): A voluntary policy targeting children under 12 years, requiring advertisements to promote healthy lifestyle habits but not prohibiting persuasive techniques. 7. Quebec Consumer Protection Act (1980): A mandatory policy targeting children under 13 years, prohibiting advertising of products primarily consumed by children using characters or themes designed to appeal to them. 8. San Francisco Healthy Food Incentives Ordinance (2011): A mandatory policy targeting fast food restaurants, prohibiting the use of free toys or incentives for meals that do not meet nutrition criteria. 9. South Korea’s Special Act on Safety Management of Children’s Dietary Life (2010): A mandatory policy targeting children aged 4–18 years, restricting marketing of snack and meal substitute products that do not meet nutrition criteria. 10. UK Content and Scheduling Restrictions (2007–2009): A mandatory policy targeting children under 16 years, restricting advertising of foods high in fat, sugar, or salt during children’s programming or when children make up a significant proportion of the audience. These policies demonstrate a range of approaches to defining and restricting marketing techniques aimed at children, including audience thresholds, time restrictions, and prohibitions on specific promotional methods.
